subject: Climate & Environment
title: Urban Agriculture
description: A fast breakdown of Urban Agriculture for builders.

hook.text: Havana, Cuba grows over 50% of its fresh produce within city limits. Necessity drove innovation.

buildup.text: Rooftop farms, community gardens, and vertical farms bring food production into urban centers.

discovery.text: Local food means shorter transport, less packaging, and fresher nutrition for city residents.

twist.text: Vertical farms use 95% less water and no pesticides — but require large amounts of electricity.

climax.text: Detroit's vacant lots are becoming urban farms — turning blight into food sovereignty.

punchline.text: The freshest food in the city might come from the building next door.

quiz.question: How much fresh produce does Havana grow within city limits?

details.summary: Urban agriculture grows food within city limits using rooftops, vacant lots, vertical farms, and community gardens. It shortens supply chains, reduces transport emissions, provides fresh produce in food deserts, and turns underused urban space into productive green infrastructure.
details.whyItMatters: Cities import most of their food over long distances. Local food production reduces emissions, builds resilience against supply disruptions, and strengthens community food security.
takeaways: Urban farms use rooftops, vacant lots, and vertical systems
Shorter supply chains reduce food transport emissions
Community gardens improve food access in underserved areas

faq.question: Can urban farming feed a city?
faq.answer: Urban agriculture cannot fully replace rural farming but can meaningfully supplement it. Studies suggest cities could produce 10 to 20 percent of certain vegetables and herbs locally. The main value lies in fresh produce, reduced miles, and community food resilience.

faq.question: What is vertical farming?
faq.answer: Vertical farms grow crops indoors in stacked layers under LED lighting with precisely controlled water and nutrients. They use up to 95 percent less water than field farming and produce year-round. High energy costs remain the main economic challenge.
